title: Runner Says Sorry After Riding on a Bike During the Berlin Marathon
summary:
A marathon is a 42.2-kilometer race, about 26.2 miles, and runners are supposed to cover every step on their own feet. But at this year's Berlin Marathon, one runner seems to have taken a shortcut on wheels.

A Chinese fitness influencer has apologized after photos appeared to show her riding on the back of a bike during the race on Sept. 27. She goes by the name Abeeeer on the Chinese social media app Rednote, also called Xiaohongshu, where she has 520,000 followers.

The photos were first posted on Oct. 1 by an Instagram account called the Official Marathon Time Integrity Unit, which points out race results that look suspicious. The account noted that her fastest time came between the 35- and 40-kilometer marks, around when "she was spotted on the back of a bike."

On Saturday, the influencer posted a "sincere apology" for breaking the rules. She said she had felt unwell during the race, but admitted that was not an excuse. "My behaviour to take a shortcut was disrespectful to the spirit of the marathon," she wrote. She also said she had hidden the truth when she first shared about the race.

The running shoe company Brooks told CBC News on Tuesday that Brooks China ended its relationship with the runner after checking the facts. "Brooks believes running should be grounded in integrity, fairness, and respect for competition," the company said.

CBC News said it had asked the Berlin Marathon and the Instagram account for more details but had not yet heard back.

More than 56,000 runners from 162 countries entered this year's race, which has the flattest course of the big World Marathon Majors races, making it the fastest. About 50,000 people crossed the finish line.
why_it_matters: Fair play is what makes races and games meaningful for everyone who follows the rules. The story shows that cheating can be discovered and can cost people trust and partnerships.

background_read: A marathon is a long-distance running race of 42.2 kilometers, and runners must cover the whole course on foot.
Big city marathons track each runner with timing chips at checkpoints along the course, which lets people spot results that do not make sense.
Cutting part of the course or getting a ride is against the rules because it gives an unfair advantage.
Many athletes and social media stars are supported by sponsors, companies that can end the partnership if the person breaks the rules.
